paper_title: Few-Step Streaming Video Generation via Condition Shifting

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Few-step sampling reduces the cost of streaming video generation. Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) supervises few-step generators with a separate fake-score network, which adds training memory and computation and must track the evolving generator. We extend APEX to streaming video by using condition shifting to estimate the velocity field of the generated distribution within the generator. The original text condition selects generation, while a shifted condition selects fake estimation using the same parameters. This removes the independent fake network while retaining S2-Avatar's frozen reference teacher, Self-Replay Forcing, and perceptual regularization. We evaluate APEX on 180-second videos using three backbone evaluations per block and a one-step spatial Refiner, with a 70-case human study and a 320-case StreamAV-Bench comparison. Compared with S2-Avatar, APEX achieves higher video instruction fulfillment on the Progressive track (3.856 versus 3.831) and higher visual aesthetics across both tracks (0.641898 versus 0.632606). Human raters favor APEX most strongly on instruction following, with +30.0% net preference, followed by consistency and video quality at +4.3% each. Motion quality favors S2-Avatar, audiovisual synchronization is predominantly tied, and usability is unchanged. Separate measurements under matched training settings show 4.4% lower peak allocated GPU memory per GPU and 9.2% shorter mean iteration time than DMD.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Diffusion and flow models produce high-quality videos through repeated network evaluations (Brooks et al., 2024; Google DeepMind, 2025; Wan et al., 2025; Seedance et al., 2026). Streaming generation incurs this cost for every new block, making few-step sampling particularly valuable for long sequences. Distillation reduces the number of evaluations (Song et al., 2023; Salimans & Ho, 2022; Zheng et al., 2025b), while the resulting generator must preserve visual quality, maintain characters and scenes, and respond to changing instructions. Figure 1 shows APEX video examples of object interaction and storytelling. Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) supervises generated samples through the difference between reference and generated-distribution scores (Yin et al., 2024b;a). frozen pretrained teacher supplies the reference estimate, while separate fake-score network learns from current generator outputs. For large video backbones, maintaining this auxiliary network adds training memory and computation. Its estimate must also track the generator as the output distribution changes, requiring coordination of their optimization settings and updates. This motivates learning the fake estimate within the generator. TwinFlow (Cheng et al., 2026) and the original APEX (Liu et al., 2026c) show how generation and distribution estimation can share network. We extend APEXs condition shifting to streaming video: the original text condition selects generation, and its shifted version selects fake estimator trained on outputs for the same prompt. The two roles share model parameters and, by default, optimizer states, while separate frozen pretrained teacher provides the same reference guidance as in S2-Avatar. Streaming video requires the estimator to track outputs generated with causal history. We integrate condition shifting into S2-Avatars Self-Replay Forcing (SRF), which trains on replayed segments of the models own generated sequences (Zhang et al., 2026c). We retain S2s replay procedure and perceptual regularization, as described in Section 3 . We evaluate APEX on 180-second videos through 70-case human study and all 320 StreamAV-Bench scenarios. Relative to S2-Avatar, APEX receives positive net human preference for instruction following, consistency, and video quality, and achieves higher video instruction-fulfillment scores and visual aesthetics on both benchmark tracks. separate measurement under matched training settings shows 4.4% lower peak allocated GPU memory and 9.2% shorter mean iteration time than DMD. Instruction-following preference also remains positive at 2 backbone NFE. Section 4 also reports audiovisual synchronization, motion quality, and usability. The paper makes three contributions to few-step streaming video generation: 1. Shared-network estimation through condition shifting. We learn the fake velocity within the generator while retaining frozen reference teacher and removing the independent fake network. 2. Integration with Self-Replay Forcing. We apply condition-shifted estimation to the outputs of S2s Self-Replay Forcing, retaining its replay procedure and perceptual regularization. 3. Video quality and training efficiency. We evaluate 180-second generation on 70 paired cases and all 320 StreamAV-Bench scenarios, alongside training-cost and sampling comparisons.

sections.title: 4 Evaluation
sections.content: We evaluate 180-second streaming generation on ten StreamAV-Bench metrics and five human-preference dimensions, complemented by absolute ratings, usability, and training-cost and sampling comparisons. 4.1 Setting Training data and model. We reuse S2-Avatars complete training data and preparation pipeline (Zhang et al., 2026c), including filtering and annotation, for livestreams, talking heads, film and television, solo dance, and 2D/3D animation, as summarized in Appendix . APEX uses its causal audiovisual backbone and Self-Replay Forcing, sharing parameters and, by default, AdamW states for generator and fake updates. Inference. Unless otherwise specified, both models use 3 backbone denoising function evaluations (NFE) per generated block, excluding KV-cache encoding and updates. The common one-step 2 spatial Refiner is counted separately. StreamAV-Bench outputs have resolution 1344 768. StreamAV-Bench. Following the experimental setup of Vidu S2 (Zhang et al., 2026c), we use all 160 Progressive and 160 Interactive scenarios of StreamAV-Bench (Liu et al., 2026f). The metrics cover instruction fulfillment (VIF, AIF), visual quality and aesthetics (VQ, VA), audio quality (AQ, PQ), audiovisual alignment and synchronization (AVAlign, AVSync), and subject and background consistency (SC, BC). All metrics are higher-is-better except AVSync, which measures temporal offset error in seconds. The 12-model comparison uses Progressive cases for VIF, AIF, SC, and BC, and both tracks for the remaining metrics. Human evaluation. sections.title: 4.2 Results
sections.content: Qualitative comparison. Figure 3 compares 3-NFE I2V outputs using the same reference images and timestamps. APEX retains both bags late in one sequence and moves the tube toward the other hand for the applying instruction in another, illustrating object persistence and prompt-directed change in hand pose. Benchmark results. APEX ranks first on VA, VIF, and AIF and second on VQ among the 12 models with available results in Table 1 . In Table 2 , VIF, AIF, and VA improve on both tracks, with Progressive VIF and AIF increasing by 0.025 and 0.067. VQ rises on Progressive (+0.049) but falls on Interactive (0.070), yielding 0.011 overall. BC shows the opposite track-level pattern. AQ, AVAlign, and SC decrease on both tracks, pooled PQ is effectively unchanged, and pooled AVSync error rises from 1.319 to 1.341 s. These results show instruction and aesthetic gains alongside visual and audiovisual trade-offs. Human evaluation. Figure 4 and Table 3 show the strongest preference for instruction following: 22 wins, 47 ties, and 1 loss yield +30.0% net preference, with MOS of 4.17 versus 3.99. Consistency and video quality each receive +4.3%, corresponding to three net wins. Audiovisual synchronization is tied in 69 of 70 pairs, with one loss (1.4%) and MOS of 4.23 versus 4.26. Motion quality favors S2-Avatar (8.6%). Both models meet the usability criterion for 62 of 70 evaluated I2V sequences (88.6%).

sections.title: A Related Work
sections.content: A.1 Consistency and Trajectory-Based Generation Diffusion (Ho et al., 2020; Song et al., 2020; Karras et al., 2022) and flow matching (Lipman et al., 2022) generate samples by integrating learned velocity field from noise to data. Embedded Representation Warmup (Liu et al., 2025a) improves training efficiency by aligning early model layers with pretrained encoder before full generative training. Consistency and trajectory-based methods train the model to predict over time interval, allowing generation with fewer network evaluations. Consistency Models (CMs) (Song et al., 2023; Lu & Song, 2024) learn to map points on the same trajectory to common endpoint. Scoreregularized continuous-time consistency (rCM) combines consistency training with score-based distribution matching for large-scale diffusion distillation (Zheng et al., 2025b). MeanFlow (Geng et al., 2025) predicts the average velocity over an interval, while Transition Models (TiM) (Wang et al., 2025) learn the transition between its endpoints. DuMo (Sun et al., 2026b) jointly predicts local velocity and flow map with two heads on shared backbone. UCGM (Sun et al., 2025b) interpolates between generative training objectives. A.2 Distribution Matching and Adversarial Training Few-step generation also benefits from direct feedback on the generated distribution. External correction signals can come from auxiliary score models, as in distribution matching (Yin et al., 2024b;a), or from discriminators used in adversarial refiners (Kim et al., 2023; Sauer et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2025a). Additional networks increase memory use and update cost. Some early distillation methods also use precomputed teacher-student pairs for regularization, while DMD2 removes that paired-data requirement (Yin et al., 2024a). Direct Discriminative Optimization (DDO) (Zheng et al., 2025a) expresses the GAN discriminator as likelihood ratio constructed from the target and fixed reference model. TwinFlow (Cheng et al., 2026) learns real and fake trajectories within shared model and uses their velocity discrepancy to construct an internal correction signal. LLaDA-Image Turbo (Chen et al., 2026a) adapts TwinFlow-based distillation to support image generation in two to four sampling steps. APEX (Liu et al., 2026c) follows this line and separates the branches through condition shifting. The shifted condition selects the fake estimator for samples generated with the original prompt. In Section 3.2 , our video formulation shares generator and fake parameters while retaining S2s frozen reference teacher. Intrinsic Distribution Matching (IDM) (Liu et al., 2026a) adds feature mean and standard deviation matching to DMD using the generators exponential moving average (EMA) copy. Few-step score identity distillation (SiD) (Zhou et al., 2025) also studies how conditioning affects distribution matching. Its Zero-CFG strategy removes text conditioning from the fake-score network, while Anti-CFG applies negative classifier-free guidance by combining conditional and unconditional predictions. These strategies modify the fake-score estimate. APEX fits the fake velocity under shifted text. Fake-Score-network-Free DMD (FSF-DMD) (Kim et al., 2026a) replaces the auxiliary fake-score network with generator-induced endpoint pseudo-velocity. APEX instead learns the fake velocity through flow matching on generated samples under shifted condition. TBSM (Sun et al., 2026a) constructs regression targets from attraction to real samples and repulsion from generated samples under an energy-distance objective; its correction is defined by sample interactions rather than real/fake velocity difference. A.3 Causal Streaming Video Autoregressive video diffusion has been studied through asynchronous generation (Sun et al., 2025a), progressive prediction (Xie et al., 2025), and causal generation with cache sharing (Gao et al., 2025a). MAGI-1 studies autoregressive generation at scale (Teng et al., 2025), while SkyReels-V2 targets extended video generation (Chen et al., 2025). FIFO-Diffusion (Kim et al., 2024) and StreamingT2V (Henschel et al., 2025) also investigate extending video generation beyond short clip. Later predictions depend on generated history. CausVid distills bidirectional video diffusion into an autoregressive model (Yin et al., 2025); diagonal distillation provides another streaming autoregressive formulation (Liu et al., 2026d). Causal Forcing and Causal Forcing++ study few-step autoregressive distillation for real-time interaction (Zhu et al., 2026a; Zhao et al., 2026b). Causal-rCM unifies Teacher Forcing and Self Forcing in streaming distillation recipe (Zheng et al., 2026). LPM studies video-based character performance (Zeng et al., 2026), providing setting for distribution matching in autoregressive models that animate characters. 17 S2-Avatar (Zhang et al., 2026c) combines bidirectional reference-conditioned training, causal adaptation with Teacher and Diffusion Forcing, and Self-Replay Forcing. Diffusion Forcing (Chen et al., 2024) exposes the model to noisy historical states, while Self Forcing (Huang et al., 2026a) trains with autoregressive histories generated by the current model. S2s replay procedure retains cross-block gradients inside sampled trajectory segment without retaining the full rollout graph. APEX uses this video setting to learn the fake estimator within the generator while retaining S2s causal replay procedure and reference teacher. FlowCPO (Han et al., 2026) studies offline preference alignment using fixed preferred and dispreferred samples. Preference optimization and latent refinement are separate from the APEX correction. A.4 Historical Context and Long Video Generation History-Guided Video Diffusion studies conditioning on past video (Song et al., 2025), while Grounded Forcing separates persistent semantics from recent dynamics (Chen et al., 2026b). LongLive (Yang et al., 2025a) and Rolling Forcing (Liu et al., 2025b) target real-time long video generation; Infinity-RoPE investigates action control under autoregressive self-rollout (Yesiltepe et al., 2026). UltraViCo (Zhao et al., 2026a) addresses length extrapolation by suppressing attention dispersion beyond the training window, providing complementary approach to extending video duration. These works motivate evaluating instruction response and motion quality alongside visual appearance as stream grows longer. Memory design provides complementary approach. SWIFT uses prompt-adaptive memory (Tan et al., 2026), IAMFlow studies identity-aware memory (Liu et al., 2026e), and FramePack compresses the input-frame context for next-frame prediction (Zhang & Agrawala, 2025). Deep Forcing uses sink states and compression (Yi et al., 2025); Rolling Sink studies the gap between limited training horizons and open-ended testing (Li et al., 2026b). MemRoPE uses evolving memory tokens for extended generation (Kim et al., 2026b). Attention sinks were also studied for streaming language models (Xiao et al., 2024); S2 adopts sink blocks within its video context design (Zhang et al., 2026d;c). APEX retains this context design for its shared model. Quant VideoGen (Xi et al., 2026) reduces autoregressive history-storage costs through two-bit KV-cache quantization, using semantic-aware smoothing and progressive residual quantization. ViewRope (Xiang et al., 2026) instead injects camera-ray geometry into rotary position embeddings and selects relevant historical frames to improve spatial consistency in camera-controlled video world models. These methods address history storage and retrieval, complementing APEXs focus on the training cost of distribution estimation. For streaming video understanding, ChronoReplay (Hu et al., 2026a) organizes heterogeneous spatial supervision into chronological episodes, while Supervising the Visible State (Hu et al., 2026b) separates supervision of temporal state from adaptive selection of visual evidence. These studies provide complementary context for the role of temporal supervision and historical evidence in streaming video understanding. A.5 Audio-Driven and Interactive Video Audio-driven character generation includes portrait animation with Hallo3 (Cui et al., 2025), body animation with OmniAvatar (Gan et al., 2025), and cinematic video with Wan-S2V (Gao et al., 2025b). StableAvatar studies extended audio-driven generation (Tu et al., 2025). Live Avatar (Huang et al., 2025), SoulX-FlashTalk (Shen et al., 2025), and AptAvatar (Zhang et al., 2026a) address real-time or long-form avatar generation. AvatarForcing specifically studies one-step streaming talking avatars (Cui et al., 2026). Joint audio and video generation is studied by OmniForcing (Su et al., 2026b), Hallo-Live (Li et al., 2026a), and Omni-LiveAvatar (Zhu et al., 2026b). TurboT2VA (Yang et al., 2026) extends consistency distillation to joint video-audio generation with modality-specific normalization and progressive curriculum that introduces distribution matching after consistency training. This connects few-step distillation to audiovisual synchronization, although its jointgeneration setting differs from the causal replay setting studied here. Comparisons must distinguish joint audio generation from video generation conditioned on fixed external audio. S2s evaluation also includes external systems such as PixVerse R1 (PixVerse, 2026), HappyOyster (Alibaba, 2026), Odyssey-2 (Odyssey, 2025), and HeyGen (HeyGen, 2026). Their inclusion in S2 provides evaluation context; the APEX evidence here consists of the internal I2V comparison and the completed StreamAV-Bench run in Section 4 . Comparisons must match references, audio, duration, and resolution. A.6 Efficient Video Inference Sampling steps are one component of generation cost. TurboDiffusion accelerates video diffusion (Zhang et al., 2025h), and TurboServe addresses efficient streaming service (Jiang et al., 2026). Pyramidal Flow Matching 18 studies efficient video generation across scales (Jin et al., 2025); the present experiments account separately for the low-resolution backbone and one-step high-resolution spatial Refiner. Efficient attention methods can be organized into hardware-efficient, sparse, compact, and linear approaches (Zhang et al., 2025b). Sparse VideoGen (Xi et al., 2025) exploits spatial and temporal attention-head patterns, while Sparse VideoGen2 (Yang et al., 2025b) uses semantic-aware token permutation to identify and group important attention blocks. SVG-EAR (Zhou et al., 2026) complements sparse computation with parameter-free centroid compensation and error-aware routing for skipped blocks. S2s attention implementation draws on several families of efficient operators. SageAttention and SageAttention2 use low-bit attention (Zhang et al., 2025e;a); SageAttention2++ improves its implementation (Zhang et al., 2025g), and SageAttention3 explores FP4 inference and low-bit training (Zhang et al., 2025d). SageBwd further studies trainable low-bit attention (Zhang et al., 2026b). SpargeAttention studies sparse attention without additional training (Zhang et al., 2025f), while SpargeAttention2 uses trainable masking and distillation (Zhang et al., 2026e). SLA and SLA2 combine sparse and linear attention. SLA2 incorporates learnable routing together with quantization-aware training (Zhang et al., 2025c; 2026f). At the linear-layer level, 6Bit-Diffusion (Su et al., 2026a) dynamically allocates NVFP4 and INT8 precision according to quantization sensitivity and reuses temporally stable block residuals. Speculative Decoding for Autoregressive Video Generation (Hu & Zhang, 2026) uses smaller model to draft video blocks and quality router to decide which blocks require regeneration by the larger target model. Both affect inference computation, separate consideration from the number of networks maintained during distillation. S2 also draws on block-level low-bit computation (Zhang et al., 2025i) and Ulysses-style parallelism (Jacobs et al., 2023). These operators, precision choices, and parallel schedules can change latency at the same NFE. The training-cost comparison in Figure 5 measures APEX and DMD under matched settings. A.7 Streaming Video Editing StreamDiffusionV2 studies dynamic interactive video generation (Feng et al., 2025). LiveEdit (Wang et al., 2026), JoyAI-Video-Edit (Xiao et al., 2026), and SANA-Streaming (Zhao et al., 2026c) address streaming video editing. These methods use an incoming videos motion and structure, which differs from I2V conditioning. Interactive streaming evaluation. StreamEval (StreamEval Team, 2026) evaluates timed interactions across avatar dialogue, avatar performance, world generation, instruction editing, and reference editing, measuring task execution, state consistency, visual fidelity, and audiovisual coordination. Our reported benchmark results use StreamAV-Bench (Liu et al., 2026f) and do not include StreamEval measurements. Visual text evaluation. VTR-Bench (Huang et al., 2026b) evaluates visual text fidelity separately from scene and motion requirements in video. UltraText Bench (Liu et al., 2026b) evaluates dense bilingual text in individual images, providing complementary background on visual text rendering. Neither is evaluated here.

sections.title: C Training Data
sections.content: We reuse the complete S2-Avatar training data and preparation pipeline, including filtering and annotation (Zhang et al., 2026c). The data include livestream and talking-head videos, film and television, solo dance, and 2D/3D animation, covering facial expressions, body motion, and animated characters. Figure 8 summarizes the data pipeline inherited from Vidu S1 (Zhang et al., 2026d). Single-shot clips are filtered for subject visibility, visual quality, content safety, shot stability, and interactivity. Smooth camera motion is corrected using background features after masking foreground subjects; clips with large or complex camera motion are excluded. Full-clip and event-aligned chunk captions describe actions and outcomes chronologically, using object detection and speech recognition to ground the annotations. The clipping, quality checks, background stabilization, and annotation procedures follow S2 without changes; APEX modifies only the model training procedure, as described in Section 3 . Five-stage pipeline S2-Avatar processing Clipping Filtering vision-language model checks candidate cuts for subtle edits. Filtering selects clear videos and stabilizes suitable backgrounds. Captions describe full clips and event-based chunks, grounded in objects and recognized speech. Speech Processing APEX uses the same S2-Avatar data and processing. sections.title: D Evaluation Details
sections.content: We detail the evaluators, aggregation rules, and comparison budgets for Section 4.2 and Section 4.3 . D.1 StreamAV-Bench We evaluate all 320 StreamAV-Bench cases (Liu et al., 2026f): 160 Progressive and 160 Interactive scenarios, using 180-second outputs. The Interactive track introduces five runtime condition updates at 30-second intervals, at 30, 60, 90, 120, and 150 seconds. We measure APEX and S2-Avatar. Other models VIF scores are from StreamAV-Bench (Liu et al., 2026f), with other scores from Vidu S2 (Zhang et al., 2026c). Visual Aesthetics (VA) uses the LAION Aesthetic Predictor (LAION-AI, 2022). Visual Quality (VQ), Video Instruction Fulfillment (VIF), Audio Quality (AQ), and Audio Instruction Fulfillment (AIF) use the benchmarks Gemini judge. Subject Consistency (SC) and Background Consistency (BC) measure full-sequence stability. Audio-Visual Alignment (AVAlign) uses ImageBind similarity (Girdhar et al., 2023) to assess cross-modal semantic agreement. Audio-Visual Synchronization (AVSync) uses Synchformer (Iashin et al., 2024) to measure temporal offset error in seconds. Production Quality (PQ) assesses the output audio with AudioBox Aesthetics (Tjandra et al., 2025). All benchmark metrics except AVSync are higher-is-better. VA, PQ, AVAlign, and AVSync are evaluated over six non-overlapping 30-second windows per video, whereas SC and BC use the full 180-second sequence. Track summaries average case-level scores with equal weight. Overall summaries pool all 320 cases. Since the tracks have equal size, this equals the average of the two unrounded track means. The 12-model comparison in Table 1 uses Progressive cases for VIF, AIF, SC, and BC, and both tracks for the remaining metrics. Table 2 provides track means and pooled results. Differences use unrounded APEX minus S2-Avatar scores, so positive AVSync difference indicates worse synchronization. D.2 Paired Human Comparisons Each comparison uses 70 paired 180-second I2V cases. The five preference dimensions are consistency, instruction following, audiovisual synchronization, video quality, and motion quality. Good/Same/Bad (GSB) counts wins, ties, and losses for the evaluated model relative to the reference, with + + = 70 for each dimension. Net preference is 100(G B)/70, retaining tied cases in the denominator. One net win therefore changes the reported preference by approximately 1.43 percentage points. Mean Opinion Scores (MOS) assess instruction following and synchronization, with higher values indicating better quality. sequence is counted as usable when both scores exceed 2. Synchronization MOS and the benchmarks AVSync error therefore have opposite directions. In the main study, consistency and video quality each have G/S/B counts of 13/47/10 (three net wins), whereas motion quality has 2/60/8 (six net losses), matching Figure 4 . The main 3-NFE human study in Figure 4 and the additional sampling and training comparisons use separate evaluation rounds. Table 4 groups the latter by sampling budget and optimizer configuration. Each additional variant is paired with S2-Avatar at 3 NFE, so differences between variants are comparisons against common reference rather than direct pairwise judgments. For the optimizer comparisons, shared AdamW states are evaluated at 3 NFE and separate states at 2 NFE, with model parameters shared in both settings. All replaytime sampling variants share optimizer states and sort sampled times along the sequence. At noise levels (0.75, 0.9375, 0.99), the default, DF4, and DF10 weights correspond to sampling probabilities (1/3, 1/3, 1/3), (2/3, 1/6, 1/6), and (5/6, 1/12, 1/12), respectively. DF10 favors the lowest noise level most strongly. D.3 Backbone and Refiner Budget NFE counts backbone denoising evaluations per generated video block, excluding KV-cache encoding and updates. All paired comparisons use the same one-step spatial Refiner with 2 upsampling, following S2 (Zhang et al., 2026c). The Refiner adds one separate evaluation per block to either 2-NFE or 3-NFE backbone. The 2-NFE setting therefore uses one third fewer backbone evaluations, with the Refiner unchanged. The teacher and fake estimator add no inference calls. The replay times ti and scoring time in Section 3 are variables used during training and do not determine the inference evaluation budget.
